College
kŏl´ĕj
n. (a quarter of Jerusalem, the second district; where Huldah the prophetess dwelt — Hebrew mishneh)
Latin collegium, an association. The Hebrew mishneh means second — the second quarter of the city — and the margin of the Authorized Version offers both in the school and in the second part.

Biblical Definition

The college in the Authorized Version is a place in Jerusalem, and it is where the word of the LORD was sought at the most critical hour of Josiah's reign. The book of the law had been found in the house of the LORD, and when it was read the king rent his clothes and sent his highest officers with a commission: “Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book” (2Ki 22:13). They went to a woman: “So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her” (2Ki 22:14). The Chronicler records the same (2Ch 34:22). Huldah gave the word of the LORD plainly — judgment on the place, mercy on the king who had wept — and Josiah acted on it: “he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the LORD” (2Ki 23:2). The reformation of Judah began with a book found, a prophetess consulted in her own house, and a king who did what the book said.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a college as a collection or assembly; a society of persons engaged in common pursuits; and, in Scripture, the second quarter or district of Jerusalem.

expand to see more

COL'LEGE, n. A collection or assembly; a society of men, invested with certain powers and rights.

2. An edifice appropriated to the use of students who are acquiring the languages and sciences.

3. In the Scriptures, a quarter or district of the city of Jerusalem; the margin reads, in the second part.

PROPH'ETESS, n. A female prophet; a woman who foretells future events, or who declares the word of God.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 22:14 — "So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her."

2 Kings 22:13 — "Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us."

2 Chronicles 34:22 — "And Hilkiah, and they that the king had appointed, went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvath, the son of Hasrah, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college:) and they spake to her to that effect."

2 Kings 23:2 — "And the king went up into the house of the LORD, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the people, both small and great: and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Huldah is pressed into service as a proof-text against the male eldership, and the passage's actual argument — that a nation was reformed by obeying a book — is passed over.

expand to see more

Huldah is regularly produced as evidence that Scripture's order of male eldership is a cultural residue. The narrative does not support the use. Huldah was a prophetess, and Scripture names several — Miriam, Deborah, Anna, the daughters of Philip — without ever appointing a woman to the office of elder or priest, which are the offices in question. The prophetic gift was never the pastoral office; Amos was a herdsman and Huldah a wife in the second quarter, and neither of them stood in the temple to minister. The same books that record her faithful word record the priesthood confined to the sons of Aaron, and the New Testament that records Philip's daughters prophesying also records the qualifications of an elder as the husband of one wife.

What the chapter is actually about deserves the attention the controversy takes from it. A copy of the law was found in a temple that had been running for years without it; when it was read the king tore his clothes; his officers sought a word from the LORD; the word came, plainly and without flattery, announcing judgment upon the place and mercy upon a king whose heart was tender; and Josiah then gathered the whole nation and read the book aloud to them, small and great. That is the pattern of every real reformation — the recovery of a text, grief at what it says, a plain word from God, and public obedience. The room where the word was sought is called the college, and no institution in it mattered half so much as the book they had lost.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mishneh (H4932), second, the second district of the city — 2 Kings 22:14, 2 Chronicles 34:22, and Zephaniah 1:10 where it is rendered the second.

expand to see more

Hebrew mishneh (H4932) — second, double, the second quarter; 2 Kings 22:14, Zephaniah 1:10, Nehemiah 11:9.

Hebrew nebiah (H5031) — prophetess; used of Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Noadiah and Isaiah's wife.

Hebrew sepher habberith — the book of the covenant; what Josiah read in the ears of all the people.

The margin of the Authorized Version offers in the school and in the second part; the district sense is the settled one.

Zephaniah prophesied in the same reign and names the same quarter, which fixes the location as a place, not an institution.

Usage

"“Now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college” — a quarter of the city, not a school."

"“Enquire of the LORD for me… concerning the words of this book”."

"“He read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant” — the pattern of reformation."
